messages.content: I want to develop training-example valuations that distinguish transferable rare-group signal from spurious correlations under previously unseen distribution shifts.

The aim is to value training examples according to whether the information they provide is useful for rare groups beyond the conditions in which the training data were observed. A pattern that looks predictive in the available data may instead depend on a spurious correlation and fail to transfer under a previously unseen shift. The goal is to make that distinction through the valuations; it does not assume the distinction has already been achieved.
What is the concrete performance requirement?

At 20% data retention, the selected data must yield worst-group accuracy at least 2 percentage points higher than random selection’s worst-group accuracy. That target must be met on three unseen shifts, without accessing target-domain samples during valuation.
Does “2 percentage points” mean a relative improvement of 2%?

No. Percentage points describe an absolute difference between accuracies expressed as percentages. For a purely illustrative comparison, if random selection had 60% worst-group accuracy, meeting the threshold would require at least 62% worst-group accuracy. That illustration is not a reported result.
And the 20% refers to how much data is retained?

Yes. The requirement concerns performance when 20% of the data is retained. Random selection is the comparison baseline for judging worst-group accuracy at that retention level; the node does not specify a particular valuation algorithm or selection procedure.
Why emphasize worst-group accuracy rather than just accuracy overall?

Worst-group accuracy directs attention to the group with the lowest accuracy. A gain in overall accuracy would not, by itself, establish the required gain for that group. That focus fits the aim of recognizing rare-group signal rather than rewarding patterns that happen to look useful across the data in aggregate.
Does the goal say that every rare-group example should receive a high value?

No. It calls for valuations that distinguish transferable rare-group signal from spurious correlations. It does not prescribe a value for every example or say that membership in a rare group alone determines an example’s value.
What does “transferable” add to the goal?

It asks whether the signal remains useful under previously unseen distribution shifts, rather than merely appearing useful under the conditions represented in the available data. The valuations are intended to reflect that distinction, but the goal does not specify how transferability will be identified.
Could a correlation be useful in the training data yet still be the wrong thing to value?

Conceptually, yes. A spurious correlation can appear predictive in the data used to develop a valuation while failing to provide dependable information under a shift. The stated goal is to avoid confusing that apparent usefulness with transferable rare-group signal; it makes no claim about which particular correlations occur here.
How should I read the requirement about three unseen shifts?

The 20%-retention, at-least-2-percentage-point improvement over random selection’s worst-group accuracy is to be met on three unseen shifts. It is not stated as a target satisfied merely by averaging results across those shifts. The shifts themselves are not specified here.
Does “unseen” mean valuation can inspect target-domain examples once it knows which shifts will be tested?

No. The condition explicitly rules out accessing target-domain samples during valuation. The valuations must therefore be made without using samples from the target domain at that stage. The requirement does not spell out any further protocol for when or how evaluation occurs.
So the condition concerns what information the valuation uses, not just the final accuracy number?

Exactly. There are two parts to the requirement: the performance comparison at 20% retention on three unseen shifts, and the restriction against accessing target-domain samples during valuation. A performance number alone would not describe whether the valuation respected that restriction.
Is this already a demonstrated result, or is it the objective?
It is an objective. The statement sets a goal and measurable requirements; it does not report completed valuations, measured accuracies, or results on any of the three shifts.
Can you state the whole aim without adding a method or an experimental outcome?

Develop valuations of training examples that separate transferable rare-group signal from spurious correlations under previously unseen distribution shifts. With 20% data retained, the resulting selection should exceed random selection’s worst-group accuracy by at least 2 percentage points on each of three unseen shifts, while valuation uses no target-domain samples.

For the training-example valuations, I propose scoring examples by their leave-one-source-environment-out influence on rare-group accuracy, with a penalty for normalized attribution to environment-predictive features.

That combines two considerations in one proposed score: how much an example appears to help rare-group accuracy when a source environment is left out, and how much its apparent value is attributable to features that predict the environment. The second consideration acts as a penalty rather than an additional reward. This is a scoring proposal, not a reported result.
What does “leave-one-source-environment-out” mean in this proposal?

It means assessing influence in a setting where one source environment is excluded at a time. The point is to examine an example’s relationship to rare-group accuracy beyond a single source-environment context. The proposal does not specify the exact influence estimator or how the assessments across omitted environments are combined.
Is the omitted source environment one of the unseen target shifts?

No. A source environment being left out for this score is still a source environment. That should not be conflated with an unseen target shift, and the proposal does not call for target-domain samples during valuation.
What is the influence part intended to capture?

It is intended to reflect an example’s contribution to rare-group accuracy under the leave-one-source-environment-out assessment. The wording identifies what the influence is about, but it does not prescribe a particular way to estimate an individual example’s effect.
So are we definitely retraining a model once per example and per omitted environment?
That is not specified. “Influence” names the quantity the score is meant to reflect; it does not, by itself, commit the proposal to full retraining, an approximation, or any other computation.
Why not score only by that rare-group influence?

The proposed penalty adds a separate check on what the apparent influence relies upon. If an example’s contribution is strongly attributed to features that predict which environment it comes from, the score is penalized. That is meant to distinguish potentially transferable rare-group signal from reliance on environment-linked patterns, without assuming that the penalty perfectly identifies spurious correlations.
Does calling a feature environment-predictive automatically make it spurious?

No. “Environment-predictive” describes a relationship with the source environment; it does not establish, on its own, that a feature is spurious in every use. The proposal nevertheless penalizes normalized attribution to such features as part of the valuation.
What exactly is being normalized?

The proposal says the attribution to environment-predictive features is normalized before it is used as a penalty. It does not specify the normalization rule, its scale, or the attribution method. Those details should not be treated as already decided.
Would a larger normalized attribution mean a lower score?

As stated, yes, insofar as that attribution enters as a penalty: holding the influence component and other scoring details fixed, a larger penalty would lower the score. The proposal does not give a penalty weight or a complete scoring formula.
And greater leave-one-source-environment-out influence on rare-group accuracy would favor an example?

That is the intended direction of the influence component. The score is meant to favor examples with more helpful influence on rare-group accuracy under that assessment, while discounting reliance attributed to environment-predictive features. No threshold or ranking rule is specified.
Could the two components point in opposite directions for an example?

Conceptually, yes: an example could appear helpful to rare-group accuracy yet also incur a substantial attribution penalty. The proposal calls for both considerations to enter the valuation, but it does not say exactly how a trade-off between them is resolved.
Does leaving out source environments prove the score will work on previously unseen shifts?

No. It is a way to shape the valuation around variation among source environments, not proof of performance on unseen shifts. Likewise, penalizing attribution to environment-predictive features is a proposed safeguard against the wrong kind of signal, not a demonstrated guarantee.
Can you put the proposal in one sentence without filling in those missing implementation details?

Score each training example for its leave-one-source-environment-out influence on rare-group accuracy, and reduce that score according to its normalized attribution to environment-predictive features.
Which source examples improve rare-group accuracy across held-out environments without relying on environment-predictive features?

That is the question to investigate; no particular source examples have been identified here. It asks for examples whose contribution to rare-group accuracy persists when source environments are held out, while avoiding apparent gains that rely on features predictive of the environment.
What does “across held-out environments” require us to look for?

It directs attention to whether an example helps rare-group accuracy beyond one source-environment context. The held-out environments in this question are source environments, not previously unseen target domains. The question does not specify how many source environments there are or prescribe a numerical cutoff for improvement.
If an example helps in just one held-out environment, is that enough to answer the question?

Help in one held-out environment alone would not establish improvement across held-out environments. The question is about a pattern of usefulness across those assessments, although it does not define a formal rule for deciding how consistent that pattern must be.
Does “improve rare-group accuracy” mean an example merely contains a rare-group label?

No. The question concerns an example’s contribution to accuracy for the rare group, not simply whether the example belongs to that group. It does not assume that every rare-group example improves rare-group accuracy, or that only rare-group examples could do so.
Could an example look useful because it helps predict which environment the data came from?

That is the concern expressed by the second half of the question. An apparent contribution to rare-group accuracy may be entangled with environment-predictive features. The aim is to distinguish examples that help without that reliance, rather than treating every apparent gain as transferable signal.
Does an environment-predictive feature have to be useless for the rare group?

No. A feature’s ability to predict the environment does not, by itself, establish that it is useless or spurious. The question is narrower: which source examples improve rare-group accuracy across held-out environments without relying on those features? It does not classify every environment-predictive feature.
How does the proposed example score relate to this question?

The proposed score addresses both parts: leave-one-source-environment-out influence is aimed at the rare-group-accuracy contribution, and the penalty for normalized attribution to environment-predictive features addresses potential reliance on them. The score is a proposed way to investigate the question, not an answer naming which examples qualify.
Can a low attribution penalty prove that an example does not rely on environment-predictive features?

Not on its own. A low penalty would indicate less normalized attribution under whatever attribution and normalization procedures are used. It should not be turned into an unconditional claim that the example has no such reliance; those procedures and a decision criterion are not specified here.
And if an example has high estimated influence but also high normalized attribution?

That would put the two considerations in tension: it appears helpful to rare-group accuracy in the influence assessment, yet its value is also associated with environment-predictive features. The question calls attention to precisely that distinction. It does not specify a cutoff or a final judgment for such an example.
Are we asking which examples work on the three unseen shifts already?

No results on unseen shifts are supplied. This question asks which source examples improve rare-group accuracy across held-out source environments without relying on environment-predictive features. Any performance requirement on unseen shifts remains a separate test of whether the broader valuation objective is met; the question itself does not report that outcome.
Would answering it require target-domain samples during valuation?

The question is framed around source examples and held-out source environments, so it does not call for target-domain samples during valuation. It should not be read as permission to inspect an unseen target domain to decide which source examples are valuable.
Could you say what a satisfactory answer to the question would look like, without inventing results?

It would identify source examples supported as improving rare-group accuracy across held-out source-environment assessments, while accounting for whether their apparent contribution relies on environment-predictive features. At present, the question supplies neither those identified examples nor measurements that would justify naming any.
So the important distinction is not just whether an example helps, but what its help depends on?

Yes. The question combines evidence of benefit to rare-group accuracy across held-out environments with scrutiny of reliance on environment-predictive features. Keeping both parts in view avoids equating an apparent accuracy gain with the kind of source-example signal being sought.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: at 20% retention, selecting for positive rare-group influence across source holdouts and no more than 10% shortcut attribution will improve unseen-shift worst-group accuracy versus influence-only selection.

That is a testable expectation, not a reported result. It combines a positive rare-group-influence condition across source holdouts with a shortcut-attribution limit of ≤10%, then predicts better worst-group accuracy on unseen shifts than influence-only selection at 20% retention.
Which part makes this different from simply selecting by influence?

The shortcut-attribution condition. Both approaches concern influence, but the hypothesized selection also limits shortcut attribution to ≤10%. The comparison asks whether adding that condition improves unseen-shift worst-group accuracy relative to influence-only selection.
Does the hypothesis say how much of an improvement to expect?
No. It predicts an improvement over influence-only selection but gives no numerical margin for that comparison. The 10% figure is the shortcut-attribution ceiling, not the predicted accuracy gain.
And 20% is the retention level, not an accuracy target?
Correct. The hypothesis concerns a selection made at 20% data retention. It does not predict 20% accuracy or a 20-percentage-point accuracy improvement.
Is exactly 10% shortcut attribution inside the stated limit?
Yes. “≤10%” includes 10% itself. An attribution value above 10% would not meet that stated limit, although the hypothesis does not specify how shortcut attribution is calculated.
What should I understand by positive rare-group influence across source holdouts?

It points to source examples whose assessed influence on rare-group accuracy is positive across source-holdout assessments, rather than valuing them solely by an influence assessment without that cross-environment emphasis. The hypothesis does not define an influence estimator or a precise rule for combining results from different holdouts.
Can I take ‘positive across source holdouts’ to mean that the hypothesis already identifies the qualifying examples?

No. It states a condition for the hypothesized selection; it does not name any examples or report their influence values. Whether particular source examples satisfy the condition has not been established in this dialogue.
Are those holdouts the unseen shifts on which worst-group accuracy is supposed to improve?

No. The source holdouts are part of assessing influence using source environments. The unseen shifts are where the hypothesis predicts an improvement in worst-group accuracy. Keeping those roles distinct matters: the hypothesis does not claim that the unseen shifts were available when examples were valued.
Why mention rare-group influence for selection but worst-group accuracy for the predicted outcome?

They serve different roles in the statement. Rare-group influence describes the signal sought when valuing source examples; worst-group accuracy on unseen shifts is the outcome being compared with influence-only selection. The hypothesis does not assert that a particular rare group will necessarily be the worst-performing group on every unseen shift.
Is the claim that low shortcut attribution by itself is sufficient?

No. The hypothesis pairs the ≤10% shortcut-attribution condition with positive rare-group influence across source holdouts. It predicts a benefit for that combination relative to influence-only selection, not for a shortcut-attribution filter considered alone.
What if an example has positive influence but shortcut attribution above 10%?

It would meet the positive-influence part, assuming its influence is positive across the source holdouts, but not the ≤10% shortcut-attribution condition. The hypothesis does not say what its measured effect on unseen shifts would be; it only specifies the condition used in the predicted comparison.
And if shortcut attribution is within the limit but rare-group influence is not positive across the source holdouts?

Then it would satisfy only the attribution part, not the combined conditions in the hypothesis. The statement does not treat a low attribution value alone as evidence that an example improves rare-group accuracy.
Does ≤10% mean there can be no reliance on shortcuts?

No. The limit permits shortcut attribution up to and including 10%; it is not a zero-attribution requirement. Nor does an attribution measurement, by itself, prove the complete absence or presence of every possible shortcut.
How precisely is ‘shortcut attribution’ defined here?

The hypothesis supplies the ≤10% threshold but not the attribution method, normalization, or denominator behind that percentage. It is appropriate to preserve the stated limit without inventing a measurement procedure.
Is influence-only selection the same comparison as random selection?

No. In this hypothesis, the predicted improvement is versus influence-only selection. Random selection is a different comparison baseline; an advantage over influence-only selection would not, on its own, state the size of any advantage over random selection.
If the combined conditions improve accuracy in one setting, can we say the hypothesis holds for unseen shifts generally?

Not from that statement alone. The hypothesis concerns unseen-shift worst-group accuracy, but it supplies no observations and does not specify how results across shifts would be aggregated or judged. A single imagined improvement should not be presented as evidence for a general outcome.
Does the hypothesis specify a model, a dataset, or a method for filling the retained 20%?

No. It states the retention level, the two selection conditions, the outcome measure, and the influence-only comparator. It does not settle the implementation details of the valuation or the exact selection rule.
Could you restate it while keeping the uncertainty explicit?

The hypothesis is that, at 20% data retention, using positive rare-group influence across source holdouts together with a ≤10% shortcut-attribution limit will yield higher worst-group accuracy on unseen shifts than influence-only selection. Whether it actually does so remains to be determined.

To evaluate the hypothesis, compare selections at 20% retention that require positive rare-group influence across source holdouts and ≤10% shortcut attribution against influence-only selection on three unseen shifts.

That comparison puts the combined selection conditions against the influence-only alternative at the same 20% retention level. The outcome of interest is worst-group accuracy on the three unseen shifts. This describes an evaluation activity, not results from one.
What exactly differs between the two selections?

One selection requires both positive rare-group influence across source holdouts and shortcut attribution of no more than 10%. The comparator is influence-only selection, without that additional shortcut-attribution requirement. The activity does not specify any further selection rules.
Does the 10% threshold refer to how much data is retained?
No. Data retention is 20% for the comparison. The ≤10% condition concerns shortcut attribution in the selection requiring both conditions.
If an example's shortcut attribution is exactly 10%, does it satisfy that condition?
Yes. The inequality is inclusive: exactly 10% meets a ≤10% requirement. The activity does not specify the method used to calculate that attribution.
What role do the source holdouts play?

They are the contexts across which the rare-group influence condition is assessed. Positive rare-group influence across source holdouts is required for the combined selection. The three unseen shifts, by contrast, are where the selections are compared.
Could we treat one of the unseen shifts as a source holdout when valuing examples?

That would conflate two distinct roles in the activity. The influence condition refers to source holdouts, while the comparison is made on three unseen shifts. The broader valuation requirement also rules out accessing target-domain samples during valuation.
Does the comparison require three separate reported outcomes or a single pooled outcome?

It calls for comparing the selections on three unseen shifts. Looking at what happens on each shift would preserve that distinction, but the activity does not prescribe a pooling rule, a summary statistic across shifts, or a reporting format.
What is the specific accuracy measure for the comparison?

Because this activity evaluates the stated hypothesis, the relevant outcome is unseen-shift worst-group accuracy. The activity provides no measured accuracies and no procedure for identifying or aggregating groups.
If the combined selection helps average accuracy but not worst-group accuracy, would that answer the hypothesis?

No. Average accuracy would be a different outcome. The hypothesis being evaluated predicts improvement in worst-group accuracy versus influence-only selection; the activity should not be described as confirming that prediction on the strength of average accuracy alone.
Does influence-only mean random selection?
No. Influence-only selection is the comparator for this activity. Random selection is a distinct baseline; this comparison does not by itself establish an advantage over random selection.
Could a gain over influence-only automatically establish the broader 2-percentage-point target over random selection?

No. The broader target concerns exceeding random selection’s worst-group accuracy by at least 2 percentage points at 20% retention on three unseen shifts. This activity compares against influence-only selection. A result against one comparator cannot, without the relevant measurements, establish the stated margin against the other.
Are we claiming the combined selection will outperform influence-only on all three shifts?
No outcome is claimed here. The activity specifies a comparison on three unseen shifts to evaluate that possibility. It does not report which selection performs better on any of them.
Does this activity tell us how to handle an example that meets the attribution limit but lacks positive influence?

It would not meet the combined selection's stated requirements, because that selection requires both conditions. The activity does not give an additional procedure for ranking or filling the retained 20%.
And an example with positive influence but attribution above 10%?
It would fail the ≤10% shortcut-attribution requirement for the combined selection. The activity does not say whether, or how highly, influence-only selection would value that particular example.
Does the plan specify how rare-group influence or shortcut attribution is estimated?

No. It specifies the conditions used in the comparison, not their estimators. In particular, it gives no formula for influence across source holdouts and no attribution calculation beyond the stated ≤10% threshold.
Would differences between the selections prove that shortcut attribution caused any change in accuracy?

A comparison can show whether their measured worst-group accuracies differ, but this activity alone does not specify everything needed for a causal attribution of any difference. It states the selections to compare and the three unseen shifts on which to compare them, not a completed causal analysis.
So what can we say about the activity right now?

It is a planned comparison at 20% retention: evaluate the selection requiring positive rare-group influence across source holdouts and ≤10% shortcut attribution against influence-only selection using worst-group accuracy on three unseen shifts. Its results remain unspecified.
What did the comparison show for worst-group accuracy across the three unseen shifts?

At 20% retention, shortcut-penalized selection had higher worst-group accuracy than influence-only selection by 3.1, 2.8, and 2.4 percentage points across the three unseen shifts, respectively. Its margins over random selection were 4.0, 3.2, and 2.3 percentage points in the same order.
Can you put both comparisons side by side without giving the shifts names they don't have?

In the reported order, the first unseen shift had a 3.1-point margin over influence-only and a 4.0-point margin over random; the second had margins of 2.8 and 3.2 points; and the third had margins of 2.4 and 2.3 points. No names or descriptions of the shifts are supplied.
Are those numbers the worst-group accuracies themselves?
No. They are differences in worst-group accuracy between the shortcut-penalized selection and each comparator. The absolute worst-group accuracies are not given.
When you say 'points,' do you mean percentage points rather than a relative percent increase?

Yes. The reported margins are accuracy differences in percentage points. For example, 3.1 points over influence-only describes an absolute gap between two worst-group accuracies, not a 3.1% relative increase.
Was the retention level different for the two comparisons?

The reported results are for shortcut-penalized selection at 20% retention. The comparisons concern that 20%-retention selection against influence-only and random selection; the evidence does not provide results at other retention levels.
Which comparison corresponds to the influence-only question?

The 3.1/2.8/2.4-point series compares shortcut-penalized selection with influence-only selection on the three unseen shifts. The 4.0/3.2/2.3-point series uses random selection as the comparator. Keeping the two series separate matters because they answer different comparisons.
Does 'shortcut-penalized selection' here refer to the selection involving rare-group influence and the shortcut-attribution condition?

That is the selection being compared in this discussion: the 20%-retention selection requiring positive rare-group influence across source holdouts and ≤10% shortcut attribution. The reported evidence calls it shortcut-penalized selection; it does not give a further scoring formula or identify individual selected examples.
Did it have a positive margin over influence-only on each unseen shift, or only across them collectively?
Each of the three reported margins over influence-only is positive: 3.1, 2.8, and 2.4 points. Those are shift-by-shift margins, not just a single pooled difference.
What about the margins over random selection?
They are also positive for each shift: 4.0, 3.2, and 2.3 percentage points in the reported order. The smallest of those three reported margins is 2.3 points.
Can I infer a particular rare group's accuracy from these differences?

No. The evidence reports differences in worst-group accuracy, not the underlying group accuracies or which group was worst on each shift. It would be unwarranted to assign an accuracy or a group identity from these margins alone.
Does the evidence say how much overall accuracy changed?
No. It reports worst-group accuracy comparisons only. It does not provide overall accuracy, so these figures should not be described as gains in that different measure.
Are the three figures in each series an average, a range, or separate shift results?

They are separate reported differences across three unseen shifts. Each position in the influence-only series corresponds to the same position in the random-selection series; no average or range is reported as the result.
Do we know from these figures whether any difference is statistically significant?
No. The evidence supplies the point differences but no uncertainty estimates, repeated-run results, or statistical test. The numerical margins can be stated without adding a significance claim.
Do these results tell us which training examples carried transferable rare-group signal?

Not individually. They describe worst-group accuracy for a selection relative to two comparators on three unseen shifts. They do not list selected examples or give per-example influence and attribution measurements.
Can the numbers establish that the shortcut penalty, by itself, caused the gaps?

The numbers establish the reported performance differences between the selections, but they do not by themselves isolate a causal contribution from the penalty alone. No additional analysis of that question is provided here.
Do these measured margins also tell us whether target-domain samples were accessed during valuation?

No. Accuracy differences do not disclose what information was available during valuation. This evidence reports performance on three unseen shifts, but it does not separately document the valuation-time access conditions.
Give me a precise statement of the evidence, without adding an explanation for why the gaps occurred.

Across three unseen shifts, at 20% retention, shortcut-penalized selection exceeded influence-only selection in worst-group accuracy by 3.1, 2.8, and 2.4 percentage points, respectively, and exceeded random selection by 4.0, 3.2, and 2.3 percentage points, respectively.
Given the results, I want to adopt source-only shortcut-penalized valuation at 20% retention. On all three unseen shifts, worst-group accuracy beat random selection by at least 2 percentage points.

That decision has a specific basis: at 20% retention, each of the three unseen shifts clears the ≥2-percentage-point worst-group-accuracy margin over random selection. “Source-only” also specifies the valuation boundary: target-domain samples are not used to value the training examples.
Is the threshold satisfied separately on each shift, or only when the shifts are considered together?

Separately on each shift. The decision says all three unseen shifts beat random selection’s worst-group accuracy by at least 2 percentage points. It does not rely on an average across shifts to clear the threshold.
Does “at least 2” include a shift with exactly a 2-percentage-point advantage?
Yes. A difference of exactly 2 percentage points satisfies a ≥2-point threshold. The decision does not require the margin on every shift to be strictly greater than 2 points.
And the comparison is specifically against random selection?
Yes. The stated reason for adoption is the worst-group-accuracy advantage over random selection on all three unseen shifts. It should not be restated as a margin over a different baseline.
What does adopting the valuation commit us to?

It commits to source-only shortcut-penalized valuation at 20% data retention. The decision identifies that approach and retention level; it does not supply a new scoring formula or extend the commitment to other retention levels.
Does source-only mean the three unseen shifts cannot be used to assess the selected data?

No. Source-only describes the information used during valuation: target-domain samples are not accessed to value examples. Assessing worst-group accuracy on the three unseen shifts is distinct from using samples from those shifts during valuation.
Why does the source-only qualification matter to the decision?

It keeps the adopted valuation consistent with the requirement to make valuations without accessing target-domain samples. The reported comparison concerns performance on unseen shifts, while the source-only qualification concerns how examples are valued before that assessment. Neither condition substitutes for the other.
Can we say the 20% figure is an improvement in accuracy?
No. Twenty percent is the data-retention level. The accuracy comparison is a gain of at least 2 percentage points in worst-group accuracy over random selection on each of three unseen shifts.
Does this decision say that shortcut attribution must be zero?

No. It adopts shortcut-penalized valuation, not a zero-attribution rule. The decision itself does not introduce a new attribution threshold or claim that the adopted selection has no shortcut reliance whatsoever.
Should I describe the reason as better overall accuracy?
No. The reason given is better worst-group accuracy relative to random selection. Overall accuracy is a different measure and is not part of the stated basis for this decision.
Does the decision establish the same performance margin for other, untested shifts?
No. The stated result concerns three unseen shifts. Adopting the valuation on that basis does not establish a ≥2-percentage-point advantage on every possible shift.
Does it establish that 20% is the best possible retention level?
No. The decision is to adopt the valuation at 20% retention, and its stated reason concerns performance at that level. It makes no comparison with other retention levels.
So what is the concise decision statement?
Adopt source-only shortcut-penalized valuation at 20% retention because, on each of three unseen shifts, its worst-group accuracy exceeds random selection’s by at least 2 percentage points.

Following adoption, the plan is to freeze the source-only valuations and test five seeds at 20% retention against random selection for at least 2-percentage-point worst-group accuracy gains across three unseen shifts.

That sets out a follow-up test, not its outcome. The valuations are to remain source-only and be frozen, while five 20%-retention seeds are tested against random selection. The performance target is a worst-group accuracy gain of ≥2 percentage points across the three unseen shifts.
What does freezing the valuations mean in this plan?

It means fixing the source-only valuations rather than changing them in response to the follow-up tests. In particular, outcomes on the unseen shifts should not be used to revise the valuations being tested. The plan does not specify a technical procedure for recording or enforcing that freeze.
Does source-only still rule out target-domain samples during valuation?
Yes. The valuations are source-only: they are not made using target-domain samples. Testing on unseen shifts is a separate activity from using samples from those shifts to value training examples.
Why mention five seeds?
The plan calls for testing five seeds rather than stating a result from a single seed. It does not say how seed-to-seed results will be summarized or specify any further seed-generation details.
Are we changing the retention level across those seeds?
No change in retention level is stated. The plan specifies five seeds at 20% data retention. The 20% describes how much data is retained, not an accuracy value.
What exactly is the comparator in the follow-up test?

Random selection is the comparator. The planned question is whether the frozen, source-only valuations at 20% retention yield the specified worst-group accuracy advantage over random selection on the three unseen shifts.
So this is not a test against influence-only selection?
Correct. The comparator named in this plan is random selection. The plan does not specify an influence-only comparison for the five-seed test.
Does the two-point target refer to each shift or to a single pooled score?

The plan asks for ≥2-point worst-group gains across three unseen shifts, so the shifts should remain distinct when assessing whether the target is reached. It does not prescribe a pooling formula or say that a pooled gain can stand in for performance on all three.
Is a two-point gain relative to random selection, or two percent of random selection’s accuracy?
It is a gain of at least 2 percentage points in worst-group accuracy relative to random selection. It is not a 2% relative increase and does not refer to the 20% data-retention figure.
What if one of the three shifts has exactly a 2-point gain?

Exactly 2 percentage points meets a ≥2-point threshold. Whether the planned test meets its full target would also depend on the results for the other shifts and on how the five seed results are assessed; neither is reported here.
Does the plan require every one of the five seeds to clear the threshold separately?

It specifies testing five seeds for the ≥2-point gains across three unseen shifts, but does not explicitly state a seed-level pass rule or an aggregation rule. We should not assume that every seed must individually clear the threshold, or that averaging them is sufficient, without such a rule.
Could we adjust the valuations after seeing which seed does well on an unseen shift?

That would conflict with the stated intention to freeze the valuations for this follow-up test. The plan calls for testing the frozen source-only valuations, not revising them based on unseen-shift outcomes.
Does freezing them also mean the selected 20% must be identical for every seed?

The plan does not say that. It distinguishes frozen valuations from testing five seeds at 20% retention, but it does not specify exactly what varies with the seeds or whether the retained examples are identical across them.
Are the three unseen shifts the same thing as source-environment holdouts?

No. Source-only valuation concerns the information available when examples are valued. The three unseen shifts are where the follow-up performance is tested. The plan does not treat target-domain samples as source data for valuation.
Does this plan already show that the gains persist across five seeds?

No. Five-seed testing is planned; its results have not been provided in this node. The plan states what to test and the performance threshold to examine, not that the threshold has been met in the follow-up.
Can we specify the absolute worst-group accuracies now?
